READING 7
ESTIMATION AND HYPOTHESIS
TESTING
MODULE 7.1: THE CENTRAL LIMIT THEOREM,
CONFIDENCE INTERVALS, AND SAMPLING
LOS 7.a: Explain the central limit theorem and the application of
confidence intervals and sampling methodologies.
The central limit theorem (CLT) states that, for simple random samples of size
n from any population with a mean µ and a finite variance σ2, the observed
sample mean, , will be approximately normally distributed with a mean equal
to the population mean μ and a variance equal to 
 as the sample size becomes
large.
The central limit theorem implies the following:
If the sample size n is sufficiently large (n ≥ 30), the sampling distribution of
the sample means will be approximately normal. Random samples of size n are
repeatedly being taken from an overall larger population. Each of these random
samples has its own mean , which is itself a random variable, and this set of
sample means has a distribution that is approximately normal.
The mean of the population, µ, and the mean of the distribution of all possible
sample means, E[ ], are equal.
The variance of the distribution of sample means, 
 is equal to 
 the
population variance divided by the sample size.
PROFESSOR’S NOTE
Appreciate what the CLT is saying, because it is the foundation to the
estimation and hypothesis testing material that follows.

For example, assume the true population mean of a distribution of
annual investment returns, μ, is 5% and the true variance of returns, σ2,
is 196 (expressed in whole percentage squared terms). If we observe a
sample of 30 annual returns, the sample mean, , while not necessarily
equal to 5%, is expected to be 5% (because the average sample mean is
the population mean) and has a variance of 196 / 30 = 6.53 around the
true population mean of 5%. We know that the sample mean  is
approximately normally distributed around the true population mean, μ.
Usually we do not know μ and σ2, so we use this insight about how the
observed sample mean behaves relative to the unknown true population
parameters μ and σ2 to estimate confidence intervals and perform
hypothesis tests on their likely value.
The observed sample mean, , is being used here as an estimator for the true
population parameter, μ. The difference between the observed sample mean 
and the true population parameter, μ, is called sampling error. The sampling
error we expect to observe is equal to the standard deviation of  around the true
population parameter μ. The standard deviation of the estimator is referred to as
the standard error of the estimate, 
 We know from the CLT that the variance
of the sample mean, 
 is equal to 
 and because standard deviation is the
square root of variance:
In practice, the population’s standard deviation σ is almost never known. Instead,
the standard error of the sample mean must be estimated by dividing the
standard deviation of the sample, s, by 
EXAMPLE: Standard error of sample mean (unknown population variance)
A sample contains the past 30 monthly returns for McCreary, Inc. The sample
mean return is 2%, and the sample standard deviation is 20%. Calculate and

interpret the standard error of the sample mean.
Answer:
Because σ is unknown, the standard error of the sample mean is calculated
using the sample standard deviation:
This implies that if we took all possible samples of the size of 30 from
McCreary’s monthly returns and prepared a distribution of the sample means,
the mean of this distribution would be 2% with a standard error of 3.6%.
EXAMPLE: Effect of sample size on standard error of sample mean
Continuing with our example, suppose that instead of a sample size of 30, we
take a sample of the past 200 monthly returns for McCreary, Inc. To highlight
the effect of sample size on the sample standard error, let’s assume that the
mean return and standard deviation of this larger sample remain at 2% and
20%, respectively. Now, calculate the standard error of the sample mean for the
200-return sample.
Answer:
The standard error of the sample mean is:
Notice that the standard error of the sample mean decreased from 3.6% to 1.4%
as the sample size increased from 30 to 200. As the sample size increases, the
sample mean, , gets closer, on average, to the true mean of the population, μ
(sampling error decreases). The distribution of the sample means about the
population mean gets narrower as the standard error of the sample mean
decreases, and our estimates of μ get more accurate.
When using sample statistics as estimators for population parameters in this way,
it is desirable for our estimators to be unbiased, efficient, consistent, and robust.
An unbiased estimator is one for which the expected value of the estimator is
equal to the parameter being estimated. We know from the CLT that the
expected value of the sample mean is equal to the population mean.

An efficient estimator has a variance of its sampling distribution that is
smaller than any other estimator for the parameter being estimated. If an
estimator is both unbiased and efficient, it is referred to as the minimum
variance unbiased estimator (MVUE). The best linear unbiased estimator
(BLUE) is the unbiased estimator with lowest variance that is calculated
through a linear combination of sample data.
A consistent estimator is one whose accuracy increases as the sample size
increases (i.e., sampling error decreases). The sample mean is a consistent
estimator because it is unbiased, and the standard error of the sample mean
decreases as the sample size increases.
A robust estimator is one that is not sensitive to outliers or non-normality in
the underlying data. The sample mean, being an arithmetic average, is
relatively sensitive to outliers in the data and is, therefore, not considered a
robust estimator.
Estimation: Confidence Intervals
Individual values derived from observed sample data, such as a single sample
mean, are referred to as point estimates for the population parameters being
estimated (e.g., μ). The CLT can be used to construct ranges of values around a
point estimate that have a specified level of confidence that they contain the true
(unknown) population parameter. These are known as confidence intervals.
To construct a confidence interval, a confidence level must be specified (usually
95% or 99%). The confidence level is often expressed as (1 − α), where α is
called the significance level. For example, we might estimate that the population
mean of a random variable, μ, lies in the range of 15–25 with a 95% degree of
confidence, or at the 5% level of significance.
To understand how we construct confidence intervals for the true population
mean, we rely on the CLT, and the key well-known features of the normal
distribution:
The CLT states that the sample mean is approximately normally distributed
about the true population mean with a standard error of the sample mean,
calculated as 
95% of the time, a normally distributed random variable lies within 1.96
standard deviations of the mean. These distances for the standard normal
distribution are called z-values.

The two points just listed combine to imply that when we observe a sample
mean, 95% of the time we are observing a sample mean that is located within
1.96 standard errors of the true population mean. Therefore, if we construct a
range that covers 1.96 standard errors either side of this observed sample mean,
we will be 95% confident that this interval includes the true population mean,
even though we don’t know what that actually is.
Confidence intervals take on the following form:
The distance added to and subtracted from the point estimate (reliability factor ×
standard error) to create the confidence interval is referred to as the margin of
error.
When we use the sample mean as an estimator for the true population mean, a
confidence interval for the true population mean is calculated as:
These are the most commonly used standard normal distribution reliability
factors:
 confidence intervals (10% significance level; 5% in each
tail)
 confidence intervals (5% significance level; 2.5% in each
tail)
 confidence intervals (1% significance level; 0.5% in each
tail)
PROFESSOR’S NOTE

You should learn these frequently used critical distances for the exam.
These will also come in handy during the hypothesis testing material
later in this reading.
EXAMPLE: Confidence interval for a population mean (population variance
known)
A practice exam was administered to 36 Level I candidates. The mean score on
this practice exam was 70. Assuming a population standard deviation equal to
20, construct and interpret a 99% confidence interval for the true mean practice
exam score.
Answer:
At a confidence level of 
 So, the 99% confidence
interval is calculated as:
Thus, the 99% confidence interval for the true population mean exam score, μ,
is 61.4 to 78.6.
It is usually the case that the population standard deviation is not known when
constructing confidence intervals, in which case we use the sample standard
deviation, s, when calculating standard error. This means that the sample mean
no longer follows a normal distribution. Instead, it follows a Student’s t-
distribution, so we need to use reliability factors based on this distribution. The
confidence interval becomes:
The t-distribution is a symmetrical bell-shaped curve with fatter tails than the
normal distribution, but it tends toward a standard normal distribution as the
sample size (and, therefore, degrees of freedom) increase. The critical t-value

distances are then higher than those for critical z-values, giving wider confidence
intervals, but they decrease and tend toward the relevant z-value as the sample
size increases. For example, with a 95% confidence interval, the critical t-values
for 10, 20, and 30 degrees of freedom are 2.228, 2.086, and 2.042, respectively
(recall the relevant z-value here is 1.96). It is common to assume that standard
normal z-value distances can be used in constructing confidence intervals when
the sample size is large, which is defined as n ≥ 30.
PROFESSOR’S NOTE
The curriculum liberally uses the standardized normal z-value distances
as approximations to t-values when the sample standard deviation is
used to calculate the standard error and the sample size is large (n ≥ 30).
While it’s useful to know that t-values technically should be used, they
only absolutely must be used when sample sizes are small and we are
using s in the calculation of standard error. When the sample size is
large (n ≥ 30), we can use the well-known z-values listed earlier. We
provide a table of critical t-values in Appendix B of this book.
If an exam question requires you to use a t-value, it will provide the
relevant segment of the t-table. Make sure that you are able to select the
correct t-value from a table, as defined by the area in the tail (α/2) and
the degrees of freedom (n − 1).
EXAMPLE: Confidence intervals
A sample contains the past 31 monthly returns for McCreary, Inc. The mean
return is 2%, and the sample standard deviation is 20%. Because the
population variance is unknown, the standard error of the sample must be
estimated by dividing the standard deviation of the sample by 
Calculate a 95% confidence interval for the mean monthly return.
Answer:
We will use the t-reliability factor because the population variance is unknown.
Because there are 31 observations, the degrees of freedom are 31 − 1 = 30.
This is a two-tailed test at the 95% confidence level—the probability under
each tail must be α/2 = 2.5% for a total of 5%. Using the one-tailed probability
tables for a Student’s t-distribution, we find the critical t-value (reliability

factor) for α/2 = 0.025 and df = 30 to be t30, 2.5 = 2.04. The 95% confidence
interval for the population mean is:
The 95% confidence has a lower limit of −5.33% and an upper limit of
+9.33%.
We interpret this confidence interval by saying that we are 95% confident that
the true population mean, μ, for monthly returns for McCreary stock is
between −5.33% and +9.33%.
Value at Risk
Value at risk (VaR) is a tool used in risk management that applies the idea of
one-tailed confidence intervals to investment returns.
The VaR of a portfolio measures a threshold for losses in a portfolio over a
specified time frame with a specified probability. Consider the statement, “There
is a 5% probability that the portfolio will experience a loss of $25,000 or more in
any given month.” This is the same as stating that the monthly 5% VaR is
$25,000. The statement is equivalent to stating that we can be 95% confident
that monthly losses will not be $25,000 or worse. This situation is pictured in
Figure 7.1.
Figure 7.1: Monthly 5% VaR

Several methods exist for estimating the distribution of portfolio returns to
calculate VaR. One of the simplest methods, the parametric method, assumes
portfolio returns are normally distributed, so we can calculate the VaR of a
portfolio using our familiar critical z-values.
If we assume that the short-term mean return is zero (a prudent assumption,
often used in practice by risk management departments), then the VaR for a
significance level of α for a portfolio simplifies to:
Because the full significance level α is in a single tail here, these are the
appropriate z-values:
 confidence intervals (significance level of 10% in a single
tail)
 confidence intervals (significance level of 5% in a single tail)
 confidence intervals (significance level of 1% in a single tail)
The formula just listed assumes that portfolio volatility is expressed in
percentage terms, and the result will give a value for the VaR in dollar loss
terms. VaR can also be stated in percentage terms by leaving out the portfolio
value.
PROFESSOR’S NOTE
Notice the difference between these single-tail z-values and the two-
tailed z-values presented earlier. Focus on the required area in the tail(s)
rather than the confidence level of the test when selecting a z-value. For
example, with 95% confidence, the appropriate z-value would be 1.96
for a two-tailed confidence interval (with 2.5% in each tail) or 1.65 for a
single tail of 5%. The confidence level is not enough to identify the
correct z-value; you must also specify the number of tails.
EXAMPLE: Value at risk
A portfolio with a value of $100 million has daily standard deviation of 0.95%.
Calculate and interpret the daily 1% VaR for this portfolio using the parametric

method.
Answer:
The relevant z-value for 1% in a single tail is 2.33. Under the parametric
method, the daily 1% VaR is calculated as:
VaR = 2.33 × 0.0095 × $100,000,000 = $2,213,500
We can interpret this figure as follows: On 1% of days, we expect to see a loss
equal to $2,213,500 or worse. Equivalently, we are 99% confident that on any
given day, the portfolio will not lose $2,213,500 or more.
While the parametric method for calculating VaR is quick and simple, it does
have drawbacks:
The return distributions of many types of investment are not normal, exhibiting
skewness and kurtosis.
Distribution parameters may change over time.
Reliance on historical data to estimate parameters is not appropriate if new or
extreme market conditions evolve.
The method does not work well for assets with nonlinear returns, such as
options.
Sampling Methods
To generate representative samples from a population, two general sampling
methods are available: probability sampling and nonprobability sampling.
Probability sampling techniques ensure each population member has a
known, nonzero chance of being selected in a sample. Methods include the
following:
–  Simple random sampling. Each population member has an equal probability
of being selected.
–  Systematic sampling. Every kth member from a population is selected.
–  Stratified random sampling. The population is divided into key groups or
strata, and random samples are taken in each stratum, which are combined in
the same proportion as the overall population. This ensures that the key strata
(characteristics) are reflected in the sample. For example, imagine that we
believe gender is an important factor in CFA results, and that we know 60%

of the population of CFA candidates is male and 40% female. To ensure this
characteristic is reflected in a sample of candidates, 60% of sample
observations would be selected from the male strata and 40% from the female
strata.
–  Cluster sampling. A population is divided into smaller groups (called
clusters), each of which is assumed to be representative of the overall
population. Clusters are randomly selected, and a random sample is taken
from selected clusters. The CLT will apply to cluster sampling if the size of
the clusters is large enough.
Nonprobability sampling techniques do not have known nonzero probabilities
of selection for all population members. Methods include the following:
–  Convenience sampling. Selection of sample elements is based on ease of
access, using data that are readily available. Because such a sample is
typically not random, sampling error will likely be greater.
–  Judgmental sampling. Sample elements are selected from the population
based on experience and judgment. This process may introduce biases of the
researcher, but the researcher’s intuition could be critical when dealing with
complex research issues.
Probability sampling is typically more accurate than nonprobability sampling,
which tends not to produce representative samples but benefits from lower cost.
The CLT does not apply to nonrepresentative samples.
MODULE QUIZ 7.1
1. Which of the following is least likely one of the four desirable properties of an estimator?
A. Reliability.
B. Efficiency.
C. Consistency.
2. A random sample of 100 computer store customers spent an average of $75 at the store.
Assuming the distribution is normal and the population standard deviation is $20, the 95%
confidence interval for the population mean is closest to:
A. $71.08 to $78.92.
B. $73.89 to $80.11.
C. $74.56 to $79.44.
3. What is the most appropriate test statistic for constructing confidence intervals for the
population mean when the population is normally distributed, but the variance is
unknown?
A. The z-statistic at α with n degrees of freedom.
B. The t-statistic at α/2 with n degrees of freedom.

C. The t-statistic at α/2 with n − 1 degrees of freedom.
4. Weekly 5% VaR of £1 million indicates:
A. a maximum allowable loss of £1 million in 5% of weeks.
B. that the largest weekly loss is £1 million, or 5% of portfolio value.
C. a 5% probability of a loss equal to or greater than £1 million in any given week.
5. A portfolio has annual standard deviation of 9% and is currently valued at $6.4 million.
What is the 5% annual VaR of the portfolio using the parametric method, assuming mean
returns are zero?
A. $320,000.
B. $576,000.
C. $950,400.
MODULE 7.2: HYPOTHESIS TESTS OF THE
POPULATION MEAN
LOS 7.b: Explain hypothesis testing and its components, including
statistical significance, Type I and Type II errors, and the power of a test;
construct appropriate hypothesis tests; and interpret the results.
PROFESSOR’S NOTE
This reading has various different hypothesis tests—some of which can
look quite daunting at first. Focus on understanding hypothesis testing
for a single mean before moving on to the more exotic kinds of
hypothesis tests. Remember that the process is the same for all of the
tests introduced in this reading, including the nonparametric tests
toward the end.
Hypothesis Testing
A hypothesis is a statement about the value of a population parameter made to
test a theory or belief. Hypotheses are usually stated in terms of the population
parameter to be tested, such as the population mean. For example, a researcher
may be interested in the mean daily return on a trading strategy. The researcher
may state a hypothesis that the mean daily risk-adjusted return of the strategy is
less than or equal to zero, then take a sample of data to look for evidence to
reject this hypothesis, which would suggest that the strategy produces positive
risk-adjusted returns.
Hypothesis tests take two primary forms:

Parametric tests rely on assumptions regarding the distribution of the
population and are specific to population parameters, such as mean and
variance. Hypotheses are made about potential values these parameters could
take. Then, the data are sampled to test the likely validity of these hypotheses.
Nonparametric tests either do not consider a particular population parameter
or have few assumptions about the population that is sampled. Nonparametric
tests are used for quantities other than parameters of a statistical distribution,
like mean and variance. Later in this reading, we describe two types of
nonparametric tests that test the ranking of data (rather than values) and analyze
categorized data to look for dependency between categories.
The basic steps in all hypothesis tests are as follows:
Step 1:    State the null and alternative hypotheses.
Step 2:    Identify the test statistic and its distribution.
Step 3:    Specify the level of significance.
Step 4:    Establish the decision rule.
Step 1: State the Null and Alternative Hypotheses
A hypothesis test requires two hypotheses: a null and an alternative hypothesis.
The null hypothesis, H0, is the hypothesis that the researcher is typically
looking to reject in favor of the alternative hypothesis. It usually represents a
lack of evidence that anything unusual is being observed in the data.
The alternative hypothesis, HA, is the opposite of the null hypothesis. It
implies that evidence in the data is sufficient to reject the null hypothesis. The
alternative hypothesis typically represents the claim for which the researcher
has set out to find evidence.
The null and alternative hypotheses must be mutually exclusive and exhaustive.
They include all possible outcomes (exhaustive), and they cannot both be true at
the same time (mutually exclusive). For example, a null hypothesis might state
that a true mean is equal to zero, and the alternative hypothesis would be that the
true mean is different than zero.
Step 2: Identify the Test Statistic and Its Distribution

An analyst takes a sample and calculates a test statistic from the data. For a test
of the population mean, the test statistic measures how many standard errors the
observed sample mean is from the analyst’s hypothesized population mean.
In our example, the hypothesized value for the true mean is 0. Assume that a
sample of size 60 is taken and the sample mean is 1.12%, with a sample standard
deviation of 2.88%.
Recall from our earlier discussion of the CLT that the standard error of the
sample mean is calculated as

is unknown. In our example this is 
We can now calculate the test statistic as follows:
This test statistic shows we have observed a sample mean that is 3.01 standard
errors away from the hypothesized value for the true population mean.
Step 3: Specify the Level of Significance
The analyst must specify a significance level, α, when designing the test. This is
a small probability level (values commonly used are 1% or 5%) which we can
informally think of as a probability threshold: if we observe a sample statistic
that is less likely than the significance level under the null hypothesis, then we
reject the null hypothesis.
Just as for confidence intervals earlier in the reading, a significance level of α
implies a confidence level of 1 − α.
For our example, let us assume a significance level of 5%.
Step 4: Establish the Decision Rule
We know from the CLT that the sample mean is approximately normally
distributed around the true population mean with a standard error of 
(approximated in our test with 
We also know from the features of the normal distribution that 95% of the
distribution is observed within 1.96 standard deviations of the mean. For our
test, this implies that if the null were true, 95% of the time we would observe a

sample mean that is within 1.96 standard errors of the hypothesized mean.
Because the true population standard deviation is not known, theoretically we
should be using a t-distribution, but with a large sample size a z-distribution is
acceptable.
Our decision rule is as follows:
Reject H0 if test statistic < −1.96 or > 1.96
This decision rule can be visualized as shown in Figure 7.2.
Figure 7.2: Two-Tailed Hypothesis Test Using the Standard Normal (z) Distribution
Figure 7.2 shows the standard normal distribution for a two-tailed hypothesis test
using the z-distribution. The significance level of 0.05 means each tail has 0.05 /
2 = 0.025 probability (area) beyond ±1.96.
In our example, we calculated a test statistic of 3.01. This is well inside the right-
hand rejection zone.
Figure 7.3: Decision for a Two-Tailed Hypothesis Test Using the Standard Normal (z)
Distribution

Our decision is to reject the null hypothesis (with 5% significance). The test
statistic (3.01) is greater than the critical value for the test (1.96) because we
have observed a sample mean that is less than 5% likely if the null hypothesis
were true.
The test just described is a two-tailed test. When the null hypothesis states that
the true mean is equal to a specified value, there are two rejection zones because
we would reject the null if we saw a sample mean that was either too low or too
high.
One-tailed hypothesis tests also exist, which look for evidence that a
population parameter is less than, or greater than, a hypothesized value. The
following example illustrates a one-tailed hypothesis test.
EXAMPLE: One-tailed test of a population mean
An analyst wishes to test whether the mean weekly return of a risk factor is
greater than zero. State the hypotheses for this test.
Answer:
The analyst is looking for evidence that the mean weekly return of the risk
factor is greater than zero. Because this is what we wish to find evidence for,
we should make this the alternative hypothesis and look to reject a null relating
to the opposite of this claim. The null and alternative hypotheses are as
follows:
H0: mean weekly return from risk factor is equal to zero or less: μ ≤ 0

HA: mean weekly return from risk factor is greater than zero: μ > 0
PROFESSOR’S NOTE
The null hypothesis always contains some form of “equal to” condition.
A two-tailed test has “=”, and one-tailed tests will have either “≤” or “≥”
depending on which tail the rejection zone is in.
EXAMPLE: One-tailed test of a population mean
An analyst wishes to test whether the mean weekly return of a risk factor is
greater than zero. She collects a sample of 150 weeks of data and calculates the
sample mean to be 0.15% with sample standard deviation of 1%. Calculate the
test statistic for this test and determine the decision to be made. Assume a
significance level of 1%.
Answer:
The test statistic is calculated as follows:
The critical z-value for a one-tailed test with a significance of 1% is 2.33.
Because we used sample standard deviation to calculate standard error, a t-
distribution should be used. However, with a sample size of 150, a z-
distribution is acceptable.
Because the test statistic is not greater than the critical z-statistic, we fail to
reject the null hypothesis. Figure 7.4 shows the distribution for this test.
Figure 7.4: Decision for a One-Tailed Hypothesis Test Using the Standard Normal (z)
Distribution

The example has the rejection zone in the right tail because we are looking for
evidence that the true mean is greater than a hypothesized value. One-tailed tests
can also look for evidence that the true mean is less than a specified value, in
which case the single rejection zone would be in the left tail of the distribution.
PROFESSOR’S NOTE
Ensure you are fully secure on the hypothesis test of a single mean
before moving on to other, more complex hypothesis tests that we
describe in our next module. The other tests all use the same basic four-
step process. The only major differences are in the calculation of the test
statistic and the distributions that the test statistics follow.
Type I and Type II Errors
Hypothesis tests can lead to incorrect conclusions. Two types of errors can
occur:
Type I error. This is rejecting the null hypothesis when it is actually true.
Type II error. This is failing to reject the null hypothesis when it is actually
false.
As an example, consider the “spam filter” on your email inbox. We can think of
the filter software as testing the null hypothesis, “this email = spam.”
Allowing a spam email to reach your inbox is a Type I error, rejecting the null
when it is actually true.
Diverting a legitimate email to your spam folder is a Type II error, failing to
reject the null when it is actually false.
While these errors make the hypothesis testing process imperfect, a researcher
can measure the probability of making these errors, and managing these
probabilities will play a large part in the design of the test.
The probability of making a Type I error is equal to the significance level. This
is because even when the null is actually true, we still expect to observe extreme
samples that cause test statistics to be located in rejection zones.
Statisticians tend to dislike Type II errors, where a chance to reject an incorrect
null was missed, more than they dislike Type I errors. The power of a test is the
probability of correctly rejecting the null hypothesis when it is false. The higher
the power of a test, the less likely a Type II error because power = 1 − P(Type II

error). When more than one test statistic may be used, the power of the test for
the competing test statistics may be useful in deciding which test statistic to use.
Ordinarily, we wish to use the test statistic that provides the most powerful
among all possible tests.
Figure 7.5 shows the relationship between the level of significance, the power of
a test, and the two types of errors.
Figure 7.5: Type I and Type II Errors in Hypothesis Testing
Sample size and the choice of significance level (Type I error probability)
together determine the probability of a Type II error. The relation is not simple,
however, and calculating the probability of a Type II error in practice is difficult.
Decreasing the significance level (probability of a Type I error) from 5% to 1%,
for example, will increase the probability of failing to reject a false null (Type II
error), and therefore reduce the power of the test. Conversely, for a given sample
size, we can increase the power of a test only at the cost of increasing the
probability of rejecting a true null (Type I error). For a given significance level,
we can decrease the probability of a Type II error and increase the power of a
test only by increasing the sample size.
MODULE QUIZ 7.2
1. Which of the following statements about hypothesis testing is most accurate?
A. A Type II error is rejecting the null when it is actually true.
B. The significance level equals one minus the probability of a Type I error.
C. A two-tailed test with a significance level of 5% has z-critical values of ±1.96.
2. For a hypothesis test with a probability of a Type II error of 60% and a probability of a
Type I error of 5%, which of the following statements is most accurate?
A. The power of the test is 40%, and there is a 5% probability that the test statistic will
exceed the critical value(s).

B. There is a 95% probability that the test statistic will be between the critical values if this
is a two-tailed test.
C. There is a 5% probability that the null hypothesis will be rejected when actually true,
and the probability of rejecting the null when it is false is 40%.
3. If the significance level of a test is 0.05 and the probability of a Type II error is 0.15, what
is the power of the test?
A. 0.850.
B. 0.950.
C. 0.975.
4. A researcher has 28 quarterly excess returns to an investment strategy and believes
these returns are approximately normally distributed. The mean return on this sample is
1.645%, and the standard deviation is 5.29%. For a test with a 5% significance level of
the hypothesis that excess returns are less than or equal to zero, the researcher should:
A. reject the null hypothesis because the critical value for the test is 1.645.
B. not draw any conclusion because the sample size is less than 30.
C. fail to reject the null because the critical value is greater than 1.645.
5. An analyst wants to test a hypothesis concerning the population mean of monthly returns
for a composite that has existed for 24 months. The analyst may appropriately use:
A. a t-test but not a z-test, if returns for the composite are normally distributed.
B. either a t-test or a z-test, if returns for the composite are normally distributed.
C. a t-test but not a z-test, regardless of the distribution of returns for the composite.
MODULE 7.3: OTHER PARAMETRIC
HYPOTHESIS TESTS
We can extend the hypothesis test process to conduct hypothesis testing of the
following:
The difference between two means for independent samples
The mean difference for paired observations
A variance of a single distribution
The difference between the variances of two different distributions
Correlation of two distributions
Statistical independence of two distributions
Keep in mind with each of the following tests that we are simply applying the
same four-step hypothesis test process we have outlined.
Testing the Difference Between Means (Independent
Samples)

We frequently want to know if there is evidence of a difference between the

Paired Comparisons (Means of Dependent Samples)
The previous test was of the difference between the means of two independent
samples. Sometimes, our two samples may be dependent. If the observations in
the two samples both depend on some other factor, we can construct a paired
comparisons test of whether the mean difference between observations is
different from zero.
For an example of a paired comparisons test, consider a test of the scores earned
by CFA exam candidates before and after sitting an educational course. To test
this, we measure the scores of a sample of candidates before the course, then
measure the scores of the same candidates after taking the course. We then
calculate each candidate’s difference in scores. This becomes our sample. The
obvious connection between the two samples is that the same population
members are being observed twice. We are looking for evidence that the mean
difference in scores (before and after) is nonzero to conclude that the course has
some value.

The correlation coefficient, ρ, sometimes referred to as the Pearson correlation,
measures the strength of a linear relationship between two variables. The
coefficient takes a value between −1, which represents a perfect negative linear
relationship, and +1, representing a perfect positive linear relationship. If the
correlation between two variables is zero, they have no linear relationship.

PROFESSOR’S NOTE
It makes sense that the test statistic increases with n, because the larger
the sample size, the more confidence we can have in our observed
sample correlation not just being random noise. As the observed sample
correlation approaches +1 or −1, the denominator gets smaller, once

p-Hacking
A p-value is the probability of obtaining a test statistic that would lead to a
rejection of the null hypothesis, assuming the null hypothesis is true. It is the
smallest level of significance for which the null hypothesis can be rejected.
The expression p-hacking refers to illegitimate manipulation of the statistical
testing process, typically carried out to generate a false positive result—in other
words, to fabricate evidence that a claim is true when in fact it is not true.
Examples where this has been known to occur in investment management
include the following:
Selective disclosure by managers to present performance metrics more
favorably than they really are, such as by testing only their best years of
performance data or removing the worst performance days as outliers.
“Data mining” by performing many tests until the analyst finds evidence to
reject the null hypothesis. This is likely to lead to false positives (Type I
errors). Recall that with a significance level of 5%, we expect to make a Type I
error once every 20 tests on average (i.e., 5% of the time). Therefore, doing
many tests will lead to more Type I errors, rather than increase accuracy.
Manipulating performance data to inflate the apparent risk-adjusted return of
strategies. An example is by using appraisal-based data, which have artificially
low volatility, when estimating Sharpe ratios (excess return per unit of risk).

TESTS
LOS 7.c: Compare and contrast parametric and non-parametric tests,
describe situations in which each is the more appropriate type of test,
construct appropriate hypothesis tests, and interpret the results.
All the tests discussed so far in this reading have been parametric tests because
they have made assumptions about the distribution of the data and directly tested
assumptions about parameters of these distributions (e.g., mean and variance).
We now turn our attention to nonparametric hypothesis tests, which are used
for quantities other than the parameters of a statistical distribution, or when
distributional assumptions behind parametric tests do not hold.
An example of a nonparametric test would be a hypothesis test of the mean for a
variable that comes from a non-normal distribution and based on a small sample,
so that neither the t-test nor the z-test is appropriate because the CLT does not
apply. While nonparametric tests are more flexible, they tend to be less accurate
than parametric tests when the assumptions of parametric tests are met by the
data.

The central limit theorem states that for any population with a mean μ and a
finite variance σ2, the distribution of the sample mean of all possible samples of
size n (for n ≥ 30) will be approximately normally distributed with a mean equal
to μ and a variance equal to σ2/n.
The standard error of the sample mean is calculated as

population standard deviation is known) or as

standard deviation is unknown).
Desirable statistical properties of an estimator include unbiasedness (expected
value of estimator is the true population parameter), efficiency (lower sampling
error than any other estimator), consistency (variance of sampling error
decreases with larger sample size), and robustness (estimator is not sensitive to
outliers in the data).
Confidence intervals are ranges of values within which the actual value of the
parameter is expected to lie with a given probability:
confidence interval = point estimate ± (reliability factor × standard error)
For a normally distributed population, a confidence interval for its mean can be
constructed using a z-statistic when variance is known, and a t-statistic when the
variance is unknown.

The z-statistic is acceptable if the sample size is large (30+).
Value at risk (VaR) measures a threshold for losses in a portfolio over a given
time frame with a specified probability. Under the parametric method that
assumes normality, and when the mean return is assumed to be zero, the
parametric α% VaR for a portfolio of size P is calculated as:
Probability sampling methods ensure that each population member has a known
nonzero chance of being selected in a sample. Methods include simple random
sampling, systematic sampling, stratified random sampling, and cluster
sampling. Nonprobability sampling techniques include convenience sampling
and judgmental sampling.
LOS 7.b
Hypothesis tests require a statement of a null and an alternative hypothesis, the
selection of the appropriate test statistic, specification of the significance level,
and a decision rule.
A two-tailed test results from a two-sided alternative hypothesis (e.g., HA: µ ≠
µ0). A one-tailed test results from a one-sided alternative hypothesis (e.g., HA: µ
> µ0, or HA: µ < µ0).
The test statistic is the calculated value upon which a decision about a null
hypothesis will be based. For a test of the mean of a distribution:
A hypothesis about a population parameter is rejected when the sample statistic
lies outside a confidence interval around the hypothesized value for the chosen
level of significance.
A Type I error is rejecting the null hypothesis when it is actually true. A Type II
error is failing to reject the null hypothesis when it is actually false.
The significance level can be interpreted as the probability that a test statistic
will reject the null hypothesis by chance when it is true (i.e., the probability of a

Type I error). A significance level must be specified to select the critical values
for the test.
The power of a test is the probability of rejecting the null when it is false. The
power of a test = 1 − P(Type II error).
For two independent samples from two normally distributed populations, the
difference in means can be tested with a t-statistic with degrees of freedom n1 +
n2 − 2.
A paired comparisons test is concerned with the mean of the differences between
the paired observations of two dependent, normally distributed samples. This test
can be conducted on the sample of differences in the same way as a t-test for a
single mean.
A hypothesis test of the population variance for a normally distributed
population uses a chi-square test statistic. Degrees of freedom are n − 1.
A hypothesis test comparing two variances based on independent samples from
two normally distributed populations uses an F-distributed test statistic.
To test a hypothesis that a population correlation coefficient equals zero, the
appropriate test statistic is a t-statistic with n − 2 degrees of freedom.
The term p-hacking refers to describe deliberate manipulation of hypothesis
testing to generate false positives (i.e., Type I errors).
LOS 7.c
A nonparametric test of correlation can be performed on ranked data. The
Spearman rank correlation test examines whether the ranks for multiple periods
are correlated. The test statistic follows a t-distribution for samples sizes greater
than 30.
A contingency table is used to test the hypothesis that two characteristics of a
sample of items are independent. A contingency table shows categorical data,
counting the number of sample items with different levels of the characteristics.
The test statistic follows a chi-square distribution with degrees of freedom equal
to (r − 1) × (c − 1). If the test statistic is greater than the critical chi-square value
for a given level of significance, we reject the hypothesis that the two
characteristics are independent.

The standardized residual for each cell of a contingency table follows a standard
normal distribution. We can conclude that cells with a standardized residual of
less than −2 or greater than +2 are contributing to a finding of dependence
between categories.
